An ICML 2026 paper that links hallucination directly to lossy compression under limited capacity.

Developer research on where hallucinations come from. It supports the persistence and pretraining origin, but says hallucination is not inevitable because models can abstain.

receipt.public_excerpt: We validate this theory empirically on both synthetic and real-world data, showing that hallucinations persist as a natural consequence of lossy compression.

evidence_items.explanation: This paper ties hallucination directly to lossy compression of facts under limited capacity. That is close to Marcus's stated mechanism.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv, Xu, Jain and Kankanhalli (National University of Singapore)

receipt.public_excerpt: In this paper, we formalize the problem and show that it is impossible to eliminate hallucination in LLMs.

evidence_items.explanation: This paper supports the 'in their blood' part: under its formal definition, hallucination cannot be fully eliminated in LLMs.

receipt.public_excerpt: We show that reasoning hallucinations arise from two fundamental mechanisms

evidence_items.explanation: In controlled experiments, part of reasoning hallucination comes from learned relations collapsing during training. This fits 'losing track of factual relations'.

receipt.public_excerpt: Finding: They are not, because language models can abstain when uncertain.

evidence_items.explanation: OpenAI pushes back on the strongest reading: models can avoid hallucinating by abstaining. Elsewhere on the same page it says hallucinations 'remain a fundamental challenge for all large language models' and come from pretraining on arbitrary facts.

unresolved_gaps: Most of the compression results are theoretical or come from synthetic or controlled settings, not from frontier chatbots.
Researchers also point to other causes, such as evaluation incentives that reward guessing. How much of the problem compression explains is not settled.
